{{Short description|Professor of evolutionary biology}}

[[file:Stephen Hedges.jpg|thumb|Blair Hedges]]

'''Stephen Blair Hedges''' (known as '''S. Blair Hedges''') is Laura H. Carnell Professor of Science and director of the Center for [[Biodiversity]] at [[Temple University]] where he researches the [[Tree of life (biology)|tree of life]] and leads conservation efforts in [[Haiti]] and elsewhere. He co-founded [[Haiti National Trust]].

==Career==
Hedges has a Bachelor of Science undergraduate degree from [[George Mason University]], and a [[Master's degree|Masters]] and PhD in [[Zoology]] from the [[University of Maryland]], supervised by [[Richard Highton]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=http://www.hedgeslab.org |title=Hedges Lab - Evolutionary Biology |website=www.hedgeslab.org |access-date=April 20, 2017 }}</ref>  Before he joined Temple University in 2014, he was a professor at [[Penn State]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://cst.temple.edu/about/news/meet-csts-new-faculty-members |title=Meet CST'S New Faculty Members |work=College of Science and Technology, Temple University |date=2014 |access-date=March 20, 2015 }}</ref> He is also a founding member of the NASA [[Astrobiology]] Center. He has published over 300 [[peer-reviewed]] works including 10 books and monographs.<ref name="faculty">{{cite web |url=http://bio.psu.edu/news-and-events/2011-news/blair-hedges-awarded-faculty-scholar-medal |title=Blair Hedges awarded Faculty Scholar Medal |date=March 17, 2011 |work=Department of Biology, Penn State |access-date=March 20, 2015 }}</ref> He was elected as a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2009 for "revealing connections between biological evolution and Earth history in diverse groups of organisms",<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-members-elected-fellows-3 |title=AAAS Members Elected as Fellows |work=AAAS |date=December 18, 2009 |access-date=March 20, 2015 }}</ref> and was awarded the 2011 Penn State Faculty Scholar Medal for Outstanding Achievement in the Life and Health Sciences.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bio.psu.edu/news-and-events/2011-news/blair-hedges-awarded-faculty-scholar-medal |title=Blair Hedges awarded Faculty Scholar Medal — Penn State University Department of Biology |website=bio.psu.edu |language=en |access-date=April 20, 2017 }}</ref> A Cuban butterfly (''[[Leptodes hedgesi]]'' Schwartz & Johnson 1992), Cuban frog (''[[Eleutherodactylus blairhedgesi]]'' Estrada, Diaz, & Rodriguez 1997), and Cuban millipede (''[[Amphelictogon blairi]]'' Perez-Asso 1998) have been named in his honor.  

===Research===
Hedges has studied the relationships and timing of major groups in the tree of life using genomic data.<ref name=":0"/> This research has led to a number of discoveries including an early origin for the orders of placental mammals and modern birds,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hedges |first1=S. B. |last2=Parker |first2=P. H. |last3=Sibley |first3=C. G. |last4=Kumar |first4=S. |date=May 16, 1996 |title=Continental breakup and the ordinal diversification of birds and mammals |journal=Nature |volume=381 |issue=6579 |pages=226–229 |doi=10.1038/381226a0 |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=8622763 |bibcode=1996Natur.381..226H |s2cid=4328989 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=S. |last2=Hedges |first2=S. B. |date=April 30, 1998 |title=A molecular timescale for vertebrate evolution |journal=Nature |volume=392 |issue=6679 |pages=917–920 |doi=10.1038/31927 |issn=0028-0836 |pmid=9582070 |bibcode=1998Natur.392..917K |s2cid=205001573 }}</ref> estimates of when [[prokaryote]]s and [[eukaryote]]s first colonized land and its relevance for the planet,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Battistuzzi |first1=Fabia U. |last2=Hedges |first2=S. Blair |date=February 1, 2009 |title=A major clade of prokaryotes with ancient adaptations to life on land |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=335–343 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msn247 |issn=1537-1719 |pmid=18988685 |doi-access= }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Heckman |first1=D. S. |last2=Geiser |first2=D. M. |last3=Eidell |first3=B. R. |last4=Stauffer |first4=R. L. |last5=Kardos |first5=N. L. |last6=Hedges |first6=S. B. |date=August 10, 2001 |title=Molecular evidence for the early colonization of land by fungi and plants |journal=Science |volume=293 |issue=5532 |pages=1129–1133 |doi=10.1126/science.1061457 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=11498589 |s2cid=10127810 }}</ref> and the [[phylogenetic]] relationships of reptiles and [[insectivorous]] mammals.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hedges |first1=S. B. |last2=Poling |first2=L. Blair |date=February 2, 2006 |title=Early evolution of the venom system in lizards and snakes |journal=Nature |volume=439 |issue=7076 |pages=584–588 |doi=10.1038/nature04328 |issn=1476-4687 |pmid=16292255 |bibcode=2006Natur.439..584F |s2cid=4386245 }}</ref> He has coined the word [[timetree]] for a phylogenetic tree scaled to time, co-founded the [[TimeTree]] database for exploring the time-scale of the tree of life, and co-edited the book ''Timetree of Life''.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The timetree of life |last1=Blair. |first1=Hedges, S. |author2=Kumar, Sudhir |date=January 1, 2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0199535033 |oclc=268792961 }}</ref> Hedges and his team produced a spiral [[Tree of life (biology)|tree of life]] in 2015 to visualize the relationships over time of 50,000 species, and discovered that diversification and [[speciation]] are both relatively constant through time and among groups.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hedges |first1=S. Blair |last2=Marin |first2=Julie |last3=Suleski |first3=Michael |last4=Paymer |first4=Madeline |last5=Kumar |first5=Sudhir |date=April 20, 2017 |title=Tree of Life Reveals Clock-Like Speciation and Diversification |journal=Molecular Biology and Evolution |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=835–845 |doi=10.1093/molbev/msv037 |issn=0737-4038 |pmc=4379413 |pmid=25739733 |arxiv=1412.4312 }}</ref>

Hedges also has a field program in the [[Caribbean]] where he has studied the evolution and [[biogeography]] of [[amphibian]]s and reptiles with genetic data and maintained a database of information on these species, [[Caribherp]]. He discovered many new species in his work and has so far named 135 species of reptiles, amphibians, and butterflies. He also described three of the [[Smallest organisms|smallest species]] of reptiles and amphibians, including the [[Monte Iberia eleuth|Monte Iberia dwarf frog]] (''Eleutherodactylus iberia''),<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/12/03/science/under-cuban-ferns-a-very-small-frog.html |title=Under Cuban Ferns, A Very Small Frog |newspaper=The New York Times |date=December 3, 1996 |last1=Fountain |first1=Henry }}</ref> Jaragua gecko (''[[Sphaerodactylus ariasae]]''), and the [[Barbados threadsnake]] (''Tetracheilostoma carlae''). Twelve articles in the ''[[New York Times]]'' have described his research.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.hedgeslab.org/pubs_nytnews.php?pubs=nytnews |title=Hedges Lab - New York Times news articles }}</ref>

===Conservation===
Work by Hedges and his team in Haiti has defined [[Biodiversity hotspot|hot spots of biodiversity]] leading to the establishment of three [[List of national parks of Haiti|national parks in Haiti]]. He also initiated a [[captive breeding]] program to conserve ten [[endangered species]] of frog at the [[Philadelphia Zoo]].<ref>{{cite news |url=http://membercentral.aaas.org/blogs/member-spotlight/blair-hedges-saving-haitis-endangered-frogs |title=Blair Hedges is saving Haiti's endangered frogs |last=Mihelich |first=Peggy |date=January 4, 2012 |work=AAAS MemberCentral |access-date=March 20, 2015 }}</ref> Together with Haitian CEO [[Philippe Bayard]], he founded [[Haiti National Trust]], an environmental protection NGO.

==Personal life==
Hedges is interested in [[Renaissance art]], which led him to conduct several scientific studies of early artwork, including the development of a method for dating old prints<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/07/25/health/science/science-illustrated-old-but-just-how-old-making-early-prints.html |title=SCIENCE ILLUSTRATED; Old, but Just How Old? Making Early Prints Give Up Their Secrets |last=O'Connell |first=Frank |work=New York Times |date=July 25, 2006 |access-date=October 3, 2016 }}</ref> and a study on the historical biogeography of beetles based on the holes they bored in old books.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/27/science/holes-in-art-prints-help-map-beetle-populations-in-europe.html |title=In Art Prints, Clues to Beetles in Europe |last=Bhanoo |first=Sindya |work=New York Times |date=November 26, 2012 |access-date=October 3, 2016 }}</ref>
